name: GSK2881078

lead: GSK2881078 is a non-steroidal SARM from GlaxoSmithKline, built for muscle weakness in chronic and acute illness. Muscle-focused readers cite it as one of the better human data sets for a SARM.

It acts on the androgen receptor to promote muscle growth and has a very long half-life, reported at over 100 hours. In healthy older adults it produced dose-dependent lean mass gains over placebo, and in a 13-week trial in men with COPD it increased leg strength beyond exercise alone, though patient-reported outcomes did not change. Trials were in older or ill people, not people seeking a cosmetic physique.

paras: It was given in clinical trials, often alongside an exercise program in the COPD study. It is not a marketed product.

Trials reported lowered HDL cholesterol and sex hormone-binding globulin, transient ALT liver-enzyme elevations and, in one case, a drug rash. It is not approved, and SARM safety reviews cite liver injury and tendon rupture cases with recreational SARM use.

chain: Gain in lean mass and leg strength
angle.text: GSK2881078 is a SARM that activates the androgen receptor and raised lean mass in older adults and leg strength in men with COPD, so muscle-focused readers cite it as a human data set. Trials were in ill or older people rather than people seeking a cosmetic physique.

lead: GSK2881078 is an investigational non-steroidal selective androgen receptor modulator (SARM) developed by GlaxoSmithKline for muscle weakness associated with chronic and acute illness.[1] It has been tested in phase 1 and phase 2 trials, including studies in healthy older adults and in people with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).[1][2][3]

Trials found dose-dependent increases in lean mass, and in men with COPD a gain in leg strength beyond exercise alone.[1][3] Reported safety findings included reductions in HDL cholesterol and sex hormone-binding globulin, and transient rises in liver enzyme (ALT) levels.[2][3][1] It is not approved for any use.

paras: In healthy older men and women, repeat dosing produced greater lean mass accrual than placebo at all dose levels, with women responding at lower doses than men.[1] In the COPD trial, leg strength rose in men and the lean mass increased, but patient-reported outcomes did not change.[3] A 2025 systematic review of randomized trials assessed SARMs and physical performance across compounds.[4]

The first-in-human study reported a dose-related lowering of HDL cholesterol and sex hormone-binding globulin, mostly mild drug-related adverse events, one drug rash leading to withdrawal, and two cases of elevated creatine phosphokinase after exertion.[2] The phase 1b study reported no serious adverse events but transient ALT elevations.[1] The COPD trial reported reversible HDL-cholesterol reductions and transient transaminase elevations as the main treatment-related findings.[3] A 2023 systematic review of SARM safety in healthy adults, written with recreational users in mind, notes case reports of drug-induced liver injury and tendon rupture with SARMs and that obtaining them for personal use is illegal in the US.[5]

The first-in-human study found dose-proportional exposure and a half-life above 100 hours.[2] A cohort in the phase 1b study found that inhibiting the enzyme CYP3A4 was unlikely to alter its pharmacokinetics in a clinically significant way.[1] Comparative in vitro work has examined it alongside RAD-140 and GLPG0492.

Three human studies are summarized here. (1) A first-in-human study in healthy men and postmenopausal women of single and 7 to 14 day repeat doses (NCT02045940).[2][6] (2) A phase 1b randomized placebo-controlled study in healthy older men and postmenopausal women dosed for up to about 8 weeks, which found dose-dependent lean mass increases and transient ALT elevations (NCT02567773).[1][7] (3) A 13-week phase 2A randomized trial in 97 people with COPD (47 postmenopausal women, 50 men) combined with a home exercise programme; leg strength increased in men (difference from placebo of about 7 percent, 90% CI 0.5 to 13.6), with a non-significant trend in women (NCT03359473).[3][8]

Analytical laboratories have published methods to detect GSK2881078 and its metabolites in urine and hair after a single oral dose, and in equine samples, as part of anti-doping work.[9][10][11] The sources reviewed do not document specific use of this compound in looksmaxxing communities.

timeline.event: Phase 1b dose-escalation study in older adults begins.[7]
Phase 2 COPD trial begins; phase 1b results published.[1][8]
